opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most useful way to frame it is that these systems aren't really intelligent agents at all, in the way we usually think of them. I've been describing them as cultural technologies. Think of things like writing, or print, or libraries, or even Wikipedia and internet search. What a large language model does, very effectively, is summarize and give you access to an enormous body of information that other human beings have produced. That's an incredibly powerful thing. Cultural technologies like print have transformed human life. But it's a very different thing from what an individual intelligent agent, like a child, does.

So when people ask, "Can it reason?", I think it's a bit like asking whether the library can reason. The library contains a great deal of reasoning, because lots of smart people wrote down how they reasoned. And these systems can extract patterns from that and reproduce them in remarkably flexible ways. But that's not the same as going out into the world and figuring out something new.

What I study is how young children learn, and what's striking about children is that they're not just absorbing information from the people around them, although they do a lot of that. They're also actively experimenting. A two-year-old is like a little scientist. They're exploring, trying things out, seeing what happens, building causal models of how the world works, and revising those models when the evidence surprises them. That kind of truth-seeking engagement with an external world is exactly what these models are not doing. They're trained to predict the next token in a body of text, not to find out what's actually true about the world.

In some of our experiments, we've compared children and models on things like discovering a novel causal relationship, figuring out which block makes a machine light up, or inventing a new use for a tool. The models are very good at things like "what do you usually do with a hammer?", because that's in the text. They're much worse at "you don't have a hammer, what could you use instead to pound in this nail?", which requires reasoning about the causal properties of objects in a new way. And four-year-olds are quite good at that.

So the limitation isn't that they're dumb. It's that they're a particular kind of thing. They're superb at imitation and transmission, which is one half of what makes human culture work. What they don't have is the other half: innovation, exploration, the drive to go out and discover something that nobody has written down yet. And I'd add that we shouldn't think of intelligence as one single quantity that a system has more or less of. There are lots of different kinds of intelligence, and they often trade off against each other. The question isn't whether AI is smarter than us. It's what kind of tool it is and how we should use it, the way we had to figure out new norms and institutions for print or for the internet.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts models’ text-based pattern reproduction with children’s exploration, but does not describe a learned procedure analogous to a child applying a taught multiplication formula.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim about reproducing mathematical reasoning or struggling with basic arithmetic.

r003.rationale: It identifies difficulty discovering novel causal relationships and figuring out something new that has not been written down.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't actually think the right way to think about these systems is as agents that reason, or fail to reason, in the way that a human child or even a chimpanzee reasons. I've argued that we should think of large language models as cultural technologies, more like writing or print or libraries or the internet, than as intelligent agents. What they're doing, and doing remarkably well, is extracting and summarizing and recombining information that is already in the vast corpus of things human beings have said and written. That's a genuinely important thing to be able to do. Culture is what makes us distinctive as a species. But it's a very different thing from going out into the world and figuring out how it works.

So when people ask about the limitations of their reasoning, my answer is that the systems were never designed to do the thing we usually mean by reasoning, which is building a model of the world and then testing that model against what actually happens. A four-year-old does that constantly. She has a theory about why the toy lights up, she pokes at it, it doesn't light up, and she revises. That's what we've called the theory theory, the idea that children are little scientists. And crucially, she's getting data from the world, not just from what other people have said. The language models get all of their data from the output of other minds. They're second-order. They're learning about the world only through the window of what people have already said about it.

Now, that explains a lot of the characteristic failures. When the models confabulate, or when they give you something that sounds fluent and plausible but is wrong, that's exactly what you'd expect from a system that's optimized for what people tend to say rather than for what's true. Those usually line up, because people usually say true things, but when they come apart, the model has no independent way to check. It can't run an experiment. It isn't acting in the world and getting feedback from the world. And I think that's much more fundamental than the question of whether you can get them to do a logic puzzle or a chain-of-thought problem. You can patch those. What you can't patch, without a different kind of system, is the lack of what I'd call truth-seeking, the motivation and the capacity to find out what's really out there.

The other point I'd make, and this is where the developmental work is really relevant, is that a lot of the things we call reasoning in humans are tied up with exploration. Children are extraordinarily good at exploring, at trying things that look pointless, at being curious. That's expensive. It's why childhood is so long and why kids are so useless from an evolutionary point of view for so many years. But it's the thing that lets you discover something genuinely new, rather than just recombining what's already there. The current systems are very much at the exploit end of the explore-exploit tradeoff. They give you the most likely answer. And the most likely answer is, almost by definition, not the discovery.

So I'd say the limitation isn't that they're bad at reasoning. It's that they're excellent at something else, and we keep mistaking the something else for reasoning because it comes out in fluent sentences.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to say is that we don’t really have a very good account of what we mean by reasoning. There are quite different things that get bundled together under that word. And these systems have been remarkably successful at some of them.

The distinction I find useful is between learning from the cultural information that other people have produced and figuring out how the world works by acting on it. Language models are extraordinarily good at the first. They’ve absorbed an enormous amount of what human beings have written, and they can find patterns in that material that allow them to do surprising things.

But think about a small child trying to figure out how a new toy works. The child can form a hypothesis, intervene, see what happens, and then try something else. Crucially, the child can decide which experiment would be informative. That capacity to actively explore the world—to generate evidence rather than simply learn from evidence that’s already there—is much less clearly present in these systems.

Now, that doesn’t mean it couldn’t be. You could build systems that combine language models with those kinds of capacities. But producing a convincing account of how to solve a problem and reliably discovering a solution to a new problem are different achievements. We should be careful about using success at one as evidence for the other.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning from cultural information with actively exploring the world, but does not characterize AI reasoning as applying a learned procedure or compare it to a child using a taught multiplication formula.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss mathematical reasoning or arithmetic ability.

r003.rationale: It describes difficulty actively generating evidence and reliably solving new problems, but does not identify generating novel relationships as a limitation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between being able to produce the kinds of answers that a person would produce and being able to figure out how the world works. Those can overlap, but they’re different achievements.

A large language model learns from this extraordinary accumulation of human language. That’s a remarkable resource, because language contains the results of an enormous amount of human thought. But think about what a child does. A child doesn’t just absorb what people say. She intervenes in the world. She tries something, sees what happens, changes her mind, and tries something else. That process lets her distinguish between different possible explanations.

If you’re learning from what people have already said, you can pick up causal knowledge. But it’s harder to tell when you’ve learned a causal structure that will work in a new situation and when you’ve learned a pattern that happens to work in the situations you’ve encountered.

So I wouldn’t say these systems can’t reason. I think that’s too sweeping. The interesting question is what kinds of reasoning they can do reliably, and what happens when they need to discover something that isn’t already implicit in their training. For that, exploration and experimentation seem terribly important.
